attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post. He paraphrases Toner's account, but the accuracy judgement ('seems to be accurate') is his own.

semantics.note: The drafter's wording matches the statement and keeps the 'seems' qualifier. But the accuracy judgement is hedged: 'seems to be accurate' signals less than full confidence, so under policy it is graded confidence and is not scored.

contract.note: The contract treats 'seems accurate' as a scoreable factual claim on a plain reading. Policy says plain readings apply only to firm language, never to hedged language. Whether the claim gets scored at all depends on that choice, which the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: OpenAI's March 2024 summary of the WilmerHale review attributes the firing to a loss of trust, not product-safety concerns, and says the board's November 17 post was accurate. It is a company disclosure, not the full independent report.

reviews.rationale: The claim is retrospective, but Marcus's judgement is hedged ('seems to be accurate'), and policy says hedged or graded-confidence language is not scored. On its face, e9 would fit his view: the review summary cites lost trust and rules out safety concerns as the cause. But that summary is a company disclosure, and the hedge stops the claim from being scored either way.
